message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a residential tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; for specific situations you may want to consult an attorney or your local tenant‑rights organization.) | Category | What the law says | Practical Tips | |----------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to **one month’s rent** for a furnished unit and **two months’ rent** for an unfurnished unit.
• Must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions (repairs, cleaning, unpaid rent). | • Get a written receipt and keep a copy of the lease.
• Take photos of the unit before moving in and after moving out. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must keep the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (e.g., plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity).
• Repairs must be made within a reasonable time after notice. | • Report problems in writing (email or text) and keep a copy.
• If repairs are not made, you may withhold rent or pay for repairs and deduct from rent (but do so carefully). | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are reasonable. | • Keep records of all payments (bank statements, receipts). | | **Entry Rights** | • Landlord must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hrs) before entering, except in emergencies. | • Ask for a written notice of entry. | | **Discrimination** | • Texas law (and federal Fair Housing Act) prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | • If you suspect discrimination, file a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party may terminate a month‑to‑month lease with **30 days’ written notice**.
• For fixed‑term leases, you must follow the lease terms or negotiate a mutual release. | • Provide written notice and keep a copy. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must follow the Texas **eviction procedure** (notice, court filing, judgment).
• You have the right to contest the eviction in court. | • Respond promptly to any eviction notice. | | **Privacy** | • Landlord cannot enter without notice, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of any entries. | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major defect, you may pay for the repair and deduct the cost from rent, but you must follow the proper procedure (written notice, receipts). | • Document the defect and your repair costs. | | **Subletting** | • The lease may restrict subletting; if it does, you need landlord approval. | • Get written permission before subletting. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities. | • Verify utility responsibilities in writing. | | **Tenant Insurance** | • Texas law does not require renters’ insurance, but it’s highly recommended. | • Consider a policy covering personal property and liability. | ### Quick Checklist for Tenants 1. **Read Your Lease Carefully** – All obligations and rights are spelled out there. 2. **Document Everything** – Photos, videos, written notices, and receipts. 3. **Know the Notice Periods** – 24 hrs for entry, 30 days for lease termination. 4. **Keep Records of Repairs** – Written requests, dates, and outcomes. 5. **Know Your Local Resources** – * Texas Commission on Human Rights (discrimination complaints) * Texas Attorney General’s Office (tenant‑landlord disputes) * Local tenant‑rights groups or legal aid clinics. --- #### When to Seek Legal Help - **Unlawful Eviction** or harassment. - **Discrimination** or retaliation. - **Large Security Deposit Deductions** you believe are unjust. - **Complex Lease Disputes** (e.g., subletting, lease renewal). A qualified attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization can help you understand your specific situation and guide you through any legal action.
